rv.q: I'm betting Broadway has never seen a greater portrayal of obnoxious grossing-out than the one Mark Rylance is splattering all over 'La Bête.'
Mark Rylance appears wearing a pair of terrible false teeth and delivers an astonishing, 20-minute soliloquy that leaves audiences in hysterics, stunned and cheering.

At the top of David Hirson's faux-Moliere souffle, “La Bete,” the astoundingly intense actor Mark Rylance flawlessly delivers a monologue — a rhyming, tour de force, just-can't-stop logorrhea — that occupies something like 400 lines of script on the page and takes at least a half-hour to deliver on a Broadway stage.

The revival that opened last night is as good as can be, zippily directed by Matthew Warchus ("The Norman Conquests") and powered by a dream cast led by David Hyde Pierce, Joanna Lumley and Mark Rylance.
While the extraordinary Rylance is the primary reason not to miss La Bete, he's more-than-firmly supported by Hyde Pierce, who'
Mr. Rylance is by far the best reason to revisit 'La Bête'
Mr. Rylance delivers a comic performance of such polished crudeness that it easily ranks with his Tony-winning tour-de-farce
But I think the last 20 years have, on balance, been kind to this script.

Rylance's drunken-masterly performance fuses elements of Johnny Depp in Pirates of the Caribbean and James Franco in Pineapple Express with more classic influences from Buster Keaton and Jack Lemmon — though honestly, all comparisons fall short.
His performance is a masterclass in comic pomposity.

While Mark Rylance's bravura performance as the insufferable poetaster Valere provides moments of genuine hilarity, David Hirson's verbose comedy proves as much an endurance test for audiences as it is for the fictional theatrical troupe forced to accommodate the bombastic fool.
Although there’s no intermission, this is a show in which you wouldn’t miss much by walking out after the first half-hour.
Four stars (****) for this unmissable jewel.
While the new production, direct from London, can't keep the play from being a windy enterprise, it succeeds in making it ever accessible and wildly funny.
David Hirson's 'La Bête' is a theatrical anomaly—a rhyming comedy that manages to be both pretentious and genuinely funny, often at the same time.
The overall experience is little better the second time around. The play is still dead in the water.
